claim: The fictional compiler opens by looking back to a simpler past when there was more time, folk were fewer and villages were proud and independent, so the record voice is itself retrospective.
source: Paul H. Kocher, Master of Middle-earth (1972), ch. VII
quote: villages were proud and independent still in those days

verdict.trueWording: he looks back to the happier past; villages proud and independent
verdict.note: Quote verbatim on the Wayback capture, and 'there was more time...and folk were fewer' is there too, as is the retrospective/nostalgic characterisation ('nostalgic about the greater simplicity of life in the old days of which he writes'). What Kocher never says is that this look-back OPENS the record; he places it nowhere in the text's order.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the nostalgic look-back is the compiler's opening ('opens by' / 'preamble') - Kocher never locates it at the start

claim: The tale closes with mock-learned derivations of Thame and Worminghall attributed to 'the learned in such matters', so place-name philology is the record's final word.
source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
quote: Thame with an h is a folly without warrant

verdict.trueWording: Tolkien ends by remarking... 'Thame with an h is a folly without warrant'
verdict.note: Retrieved from the Internet Archive full text (djvu.txt) of the item, pp. 90-91. Quote verbatim; 'ends by remarking' supports the closing position, and 'the whole story that Tolkien tells to account for the names of Thame and Worminghall is based on nothing, is mere fiction' supports the mock-learned derivations of both names. Shippey nowhere quotes or reports the in-tale attribution phrase.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the attribution of the derivations to 'the learned in such matters' - that phrase appears nowhere in Shippey's text

claim: Farmer Giles carries a two-layer apparatus in one short foreword: an imagined editor faults an imagined author's geography, though that author 'lived himself in the lands of the Little Kingdom'.
source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
quote: the imagined 'editor' of Farmer Giles to criticise its imagined 'author'

verdict.trueWording: extremely unfair of the imagined 'editor'... to criticise its imagined 'author'
verdict.note: Quote verbatim, and the continuation is verbatim too: 'that "author", like Tolkien, "lived himself in the lands of the Little Kingdom" and knew what he was writing about.' The editor-over-author two-layer point is squarely Shippey's. What the page does not do is locate that apparatus in the Foreword or call it short; the word 'foreword' does not occur in the passage.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the two layers sit 'in one short foreword' - Shippey never names the Foreword or its length

claim: Distances and directions in the tale map onto real Oxfordshire places (Ham/Thame, Tamworth, Farthingho, the Rollright Stones) at a parochial scale, so the Little Kingdom is measured like a real county.
source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
quote: proof of the 'Little Kingdom's' lack of territorial ambition

verdict.trueWording: Thame in Buckinghamshire; Farthingho in Northamptonshire; parochial scale
verdict.note: Quote verbatim. Shippey gives Ham = now Thame, twelve miles east of Oxford; the Middle Kingdom's capital 'sounds like Tamworth... sixty-eight miles from Thame'; Farthingho 'on a direct line... about a third of the way' as 'proof of the Little Kingdom's lack of territorial ambition'; Wales and the Pennines 'on this parochial scale suitably far off'; the Standing Stones = the Rollright Stones on the Warwickshire/Oxfordshire boundary. The counties Shippey actually names are Buckinghamshire, Northamptonshire and Warwickshire, not Oxfordshire.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'real Oxfordshire places' - Shippey puts Thame in Buckinghamshire, Farthingho in Northamptonshire, and Tamworth as the Mercian capital

claim: The tale's narrator was 'Daddy' in the oral original, became 'the family jester', and took on a formal scholarly tone when the story was enlarged by half for an academic essay club in 1938.
source: Hammond & Scull, 'Farmer Giles of Ham' (Tolkien Estate)

verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the narrator took on a formal scholarly tone at the 1938 enlargement — the page dates the mock-scholarly voice to the 1949 revision instead
verdict.trueWording: For this larger, more academic audience, he added many proper names, jokes, and allusions
verdict.note: Raw page fetched (200, live). Quote 'the family jester' is verbatim: 'In the second version of the story, the narrator is "the family jester"'. Supported: narrated by 'Daddy' in the first version; 'enlarging it by some fifty per cent' in January 1938 for the Lovelace Society, 'an undergraduate essay club at Oxford's Worcester College'. NOT supported: any narratorial shift to scholarly tone at that 1938 stage — the page says the 1938 additions were 'proper names, jokes, and allusions', and places the apparatus later: 'Tolkien again revised the text, and added a mock foreword' before the 1949 publication. Second minor slip: 'Daddy' narrates the first written version, not the oral original.

claim: The Prologue says 'pipe-weed' rather than tobacco because the imported word would sound wrong, and hedges its botany with a Latin binomial instead.
source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth

verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'a Latin binomial' — the page shows only the genus name, Tolkien's hedge 'a variety probably of Nicotiana', which is a uninomial, not a binomial
verdict.trueWording: Why not say 'tobacco', since the plant is 'a variety probably of Nicotiana'? Because the word would sound wrong
verdict.note: Same raw book text, ch. 3 'The Bourgeois Burglar', around the p. 63-64 running heads. Quote 'a variety probably of Nicotiana' verbatim, and the pipe-weed-not-tobacco reason is verbatim ('Because the word would sound wrong ... It is an import from some unknown Caribbean language via Spanish'). The only defective limb is the botanical label: a binomial needs genus plus species, and neither Shippey nor the Prologue supplies one.

claim: The Prologue is a richly textured anthropology of the hobbits, delivered in an editorial voice of scholarly distance, and notes that hobbits liked books that set out what they already knew fair and square with no contradictions.
source: Thomas J. West III, 'Tolkien Tuesdays: Re-Reading The Lord of the Rings: Prologue'
quote: a richly-textured anthropology about the hobbits

verdict.trueWording: a richly-textured anthropology about the hobbits and the Shire
verdict.note: omnivorous.substack.com raw HTML carries the full post. Quote verbatim: 'a richly-textured anthropology about the hobbits and the Shire that they call home'. The books limb is verbatim too: 'they liked to have books filled with things that they already knew, set out fair and square with no contradictions' (7). But nothing on the page describes the Prologue's voice as editorial or scholarly or as keeping distance — the only tonal characterisations are 'more light-hearted than heavy' and 'It's not condescending, exactly'; the words scholarly, editorial, academic and detached do not occur, and the single hit for 'distance' is the hobbits distancing themselves from the Elves.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: delivered in an editorial voice of scholarly distance

claim: Every stage of the Red Book's fictional transmission carries two datings, an Age-date and a Shire-reckoning equivalent, so the records cross-reference two calendars.
source: Alexander Schmitt, 'Stages and Logic of the fictitious tradition of Tolkien's Legendarium' (schematax.org, 2021)

verdict.note: schematax PDF fetched raw (HTTP 200, 3 pp.). The quote 'IV 172 / S.R. 1592' is verbatim, at stages (13), (14), (15) and in the timeline, and dual Age/Shire dating is indeed the schema's pervasive habit: (2) III 3002 / S.R. 1402, (3) III 3003-3018 / S.R. 1403-1418, (8) IV 62 / S.R. 1482, (11) IV 64 / S.R. 1484, and so on. But 'every stage' is falsified by the same page: stage (1) 'Bilbo has diaries containing his recountings of his quest for Erebor' carries no date at all, and stage (7) is printed as '(7) ? Sam makes his additions.' Two of the fifteen stages carry no dating, so the universal quantifier fails on the page that is cited for it.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: every stage ... carries two datings (stages (1) and (7) carry none)
